segments.text: - Hello everyone.
Welcome back to Altium Academy.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.

Today we're gonna be
talking about something
that you can do in your PCB layout

to ensure your fabricator
has the correct layer order

when they're reviewing
your fabrication files.

And that is to use stacking
stripes in your PCB layout.

Now, doing this in Altium
requires doing a couple things
with design rules,

but I am going to show you
how to do that in this video

and it's actually really
simple once you understand

how to construct a basic
query in the design rules.

So let's go ahead and jump
into Altium and get started.
(upbeat music)
So before we jump into our demo in Altium,
let's take a look at that viewer question.
Alexander Quilty writes,
"Good morning, Mr. Peterson.
My name is Alex.
I do PCB design for Fermilab.

My question for you is could
you possibly do some content
on stacking stripes in AD?
I'm aware of a Chris Carlson video,
however, it seems dated and impractical
since we now have impedance profiles
in the stackup manager,

making the idea of turning
plain layers into signal layers
to allow copper placement quite difficult.
Extra info:
currently I use pours on signal layers

and split planes on the
edge for the inner layers,

but I cannot figure out how
to allow the split plane
on the edge to go all the way

to the edge of the PCB
while still maintaining
the clearance elsewhere."
In order to do this,

you are going to have to
leverage the query system

and you are going to need
to create a dummy net
in order to apply rules that apply only
to the stacking stripes

versus the rest of the
stuff in your board.

I do know that there is a
split plane object in Altium
that you can call out with the query tool
in the design rules dialogue.
Now, before we jump in and show this,
let me explain what stacking stripes are.

Stacking stripes follow
a very simple concept.

They basically are pieces
of copper that are exposed
through the edge of the PCB,

and you'll be able to see them
when you look at the edge.

And typically what we do
is we generate a stair step

of stacking stripes
along the edge of the PCB
so that we can identify the layer order
just by looking at the edge of the PCB.
By putting on these stacking stripes,
it allows you the designer to verify

that the fabrication
house built the stack up
with the correct layer order.
Stacking stripes serve another purpose,
which is to allow the CAM department

to also verify the layer
order in your Gerbers

against any other documentation
that you might send them,

that way when they're
planning out the process
to build your stack up,

they're going to select the
right layers in the right order
and build it correctly.
Now, there are other ways to indicate

what is the correct layer
order in your PCB stackup,

and I'll go over how to do that
when we get into this demo.
But for now,

let's take a look at how
to place stacking stripes
while also controlling the clearances
within the design rules.

So here you can see inside of
Altium, I have a blank PCB,
and what I'm gonna do is just show you
how to draw out those stacking stripes

and then configure them for
use in a multi-layer stack up
with planes or with other internal layers.
So here you can see I have this board
and what I'm gonna do is just zoom in
right here to the edge.

I can use either a polygon
or I can use a fill.

So what I'm gonna do is
just use a polygon pour.

You can see the snap tool
just snaps right there
to the edge of the board.

And then we're just gonna go
ahead and place this here.

We'll hit escape, and then
you can see here it fills in.
And there we go.
We have our first stacking stripe.

Now the distance into the board
vertically is less important
than the distance along the board.
If we look in the outlying vertices column
here in the properties panel,

it's set to a hundred mills
just based on where I drew it.

Typically you don't have
to do it that large,
you could do it as low as let's say 40 mil
or one millimeter.
So here I'm gonna draw it out at 40 mil

and then we're gonna just repo
the polygon and there we go.
So what we wanna do on this first layer

is we generally make
this shorter horizontally

and then we steadily
increase the horizontal width
of this stacking stripe

as we go into more and more
layers in the PCB stackup.
Now here, this is a default stackup
that's created from a new PCB.

So what I'm gonna do is
I'm just gonna go ahead

and I'm gonna insert a plane
layer on the next layer,

and we're gonna see what
happens with the plane layer
and how we can control those clearances.

Now by default when we
place a plane layer,
you'll notice here if we go onto layer two
that we have a plane that we can select,
but then we also have an area right here

that is automatically
applied along the board edge

and that area that's
applied along the board edge

is negative to whatever
the copper is defined
here in this layer.

So what I mean by that
is this line right here
is a negative line,

meaning this is showing
you the absence of copper
that's drawn in here on this plain layer.

So what that means is that all
of the copper on this layer

is automatically pulled
back from the board edge

by this distance that
you can see right here
as drawn by this line.

And if we just go ahead
and put our cursor here,
we can kinda measure what the distance is.
And you'll see here from the y coordinate

in the lower left hand
portion of the screen
that this distance is 20 mils.

The layer is automatically
applying a 20 mil clearance
between the board edge and the copper edge
on this plain layer.

So this is why if you're
gonna do stacking stripes,

you really shouldn't do
them on a plain layer.

What you should actually do is
set this up as a signal layer

and set up the rest of your
layers as signal layers.
Go ahead and save this,

and then it will convert
everything to signal layers
in the PCB layout.

And then you can draw
in your stacking stripes
using polygons.

So here are my first stacking
strikes about 319 mils long.

What I'm gonna do is I'm
gonna reduce that distance

and I wanna reduce it to
something that I can see
through the edge of the PCB.

So I would say at
minimum should be 50 mil.

We're gonna go ahead
and make this 100 mil.
So I'm gonna set this vertex to 3,100.
I'll set the next one to 3,100,

and now we have a 100
mil long stacking stripe.

You can see here it extends
all the way to the board edge.
So why does this stacking stripe extend
all the way to the board edge,

but other copper like the
plain layer copper does not?
Well, you can actually configure

and control which pieces
of copper in the design
extend all the way to the board edge
using the board edge clearance rule.
So if go into design rules,

you'll see there is a board
outline clearance rule,

and by default, there is no
rule created in this PCB,
and that's why this stacking stripe

is allowed to extend all
the way down to the edge.
So if I click new rule
and then I open up that rule,

you'll see here that it
allows me to configure

what is the clearance
between different objects
and the edge of the board.
Here you can see by default,
it's applying a 10 mil clearance.
So if I go ahead and hit OK
and then I re-pour the polygon,
it then applies that 10 mil clearance.

Now what we can do is we can
create net specific rules
for these stacking stripes.

So what we're gonna do here
is we're going to make sure

that we have a couple of
nets inside this PCB layout.

And because this PCB is
not tied to any project,
of course there are no nets in this board,

but we're gonna go ahead
and add a couple of nets.

So the first one we're
gonna add is a ground net,

and then the second one
that we're going to add,
we're just gonna name it stripes,

and that's gonna be our net
for our stacking stripes.
We'll go ahead and hit OK.
So now we have two nets in this board.

We have one for ground and
one for stacking stripes.

So let's go ahead and go
back into the design rules.

And what we wanna do is create
two board outline clearances.
We want to create one for our stripes
and then one for everything else.
So this one that we have here with 10 mils

set by default is gonna be
our everything else board
outline clearance rule.
I'm gonna go ahead and duplicate this,
and then I'm gonna call this new rule
outline clearance stripes.
And this is gonna be a net specific rule,

and this is basically
gonna be a net stripes
and we're gonna set the clearance to zero.
Now, once I hit OK, I can go back here,
I can select this polygon,
I can assign it to the stripes net,
and then when I re-pour it,

you'll see here it can
now extend all the way
to the board edge.
Just as a check,

we can of course draw
out a ground polygon.

And you can see here that
when I draw this out,
even when I draw it past the board edge

and then re-pour it, the clearance
is automatically applied.
So that's exactly the kind of thing

that we want when we're
using stacking stripes.
The only copper that should extend

all the way to the board edge
is the stacking stripe copper,
but none of the other copper
should extend to the board edge.

So now let's take a look at
what these stacking stripes

look like when we stack
them up on multiple layers.

So first I'm just gonna
delete this extra polygon.
I'm gonna make a copy of this polygon,

and then what I'm gonna
do is move this polygon
into the next layer,
and then I'm going to extend it by 50 mil.

Now you don't have to
extend it just by 50 mil,

you can extend it by frankly
whatever length you want,

but you wanna be able to see
what is the size difference

between your stacking
stripes when they're exposed
through the edge of the PCB.

So I would say an additional
50 mil is a pretty good value

to extend the length of
this stacking stripe.

So I'm gonna do that by
changing the vertices.
I'm gonna then paste my original polygon
back here on the top layer.

I'm gonna make sure that
these are still assigned
to the stripes net.
And then we're gonna go ahead and re-pour.

And so now you can see
our stacking stripes
built on layer one and layer two.

So here if I go to layer two,
I can do the exact same thing.
I can go ahead and copy this.
I can then move this down to layer three.

I can then extend the
length of this stripe
by another 50 mil.

I'm gonna go ahead and
make this 50 mil longer
just by adjusting the vertices.
And then I'll paste this back here again.
And then when I select all these,

just wanna make sure that
they're all on the stripes net
when I re-pour them,
you'll then be able to see them
here on the edge of the stackup.
So here, if I put this in 3D

and just kind of look
through the edge of the PCB,

you can see what our
stacking stripes look like.

And this is exactly what we
wanna see through the edge
of the PCB once the board gets fabricated.

So you can see I've
copied this from layer one
into layer two and layer three,

and then we just wanna
do this one more time
onto layer four,

and that'll give us all four
of our stacking stripes.

And that's gonna be
our visual verification
that the board was built with the layers

in the correct order matching
what we have in the CAD tool.

Now, the use of stacking stripes
is a bit of an early method

for ensuring that all of
the layers are fabricated
in the correct order,

but it's not the only
way that you can do this.
Instead of using stacking stripes,

what you could do is you
could just use a text object
like you see here,
and you could write out a layer number
on each of these layers.

So for example, I could just
put a one here for layer one,
I would wanna make sure, again,
I have this assigned to the right net.
You could then go to the next layer.
You could place also a text object

and you could make this
one the number two,
and that's gonna be for layer two.

So when the CAM operator
at you manufacturer
puts your data into their CAM software,
they're then gonna see these numbers
on these different layers,

and then they're gonna
be able to make sure
that the file that they have, for example,
for your Gerber file,
corresponds to layer one in the stackup
that they're actually going to build,

and so on and so forth for
all the rest of your layers.

Now, the difference between
this and stacking stripes
is of course you're not gonna be able
to see the one, two, three,

and so on and so forth
through all of the layers.
You're only gonna be able to see
what's on the surface layers.
But with the stacking stripes,

the advantage is that
you're able to see them

through the edge of the board
after the board is fabricated.

Now, there's other thing
that you can do in the PCB

to ensure that your CAM
operator assigns the layers
in the correct order
when they're looking at your output data.
And I'm gonna show you that here
inside of our ethernet switch PCB.

So here I'm inside the
ethernet switch PCB,
and when I zoom in here,
you'll notice on the copper layer

that we actually have a text
object that says top layer.

And as we go through all
of the different layers,

we have those same labels
assigned to other layers.

You can also assign this
label here in this plain layer
as you can see on screen.
And same thing here for layer five,
we can also assign it to this plain layer.

So we can also assign
those same text assignments
over here to these other layers.

You can see I have one for the
silk screen top and bottom.

You can see I have one for
the top and bottom paste.

And notice that the bottom
overlay is actually reversed,

so that way when they turn
the board over and look at it,

they can verify that
indeed this is actually
the bottom silk screen.
So again, this is another visual cue
that the CAM operator can use to ensure

that the layer they're
looking at gets placed
in the correct order in the PCB stackup
that gets sent out for build.

Now there's something
else that Altium does

that helps ensure that the
files that are exported

for manufacturing have a
very clear layer assignment

given to them when they're
viewed in a CAM tool

or when they're viewed
in your documentation.
So here I have the draftsman file
pulled up for our ethernet switch.

And if I just scroll down
here to the stackup table,

you can see what is done
in the stackup table

to link the layers in the
design to the fabrication data
that we get sent out to a manufacturer.
It's right here in the right hand column.

I have a Gerber column for
each layer in this stackup.

And what this Gerber
column does is it tells you

which file extension
in these Gerber exports

corresponds to the layer
that actually appears
in the PCB layout.

Now, this is really nice
because I didn't have
to actually go through and manually create
each of these assignments.
Altium does it automatically
when I create this layer stack legend
inside of a draftsman file.
Now, how does it create those extensions?

Well, it does that
inside of an outputs file
using the Gerber outputs container
inside that outputs file.
And when you use that Gerber container
and select the Altium specific extensions,

all of those output
extensions are going to appear

on each of the files
corresponding to specific layers
in the PCB stackup.
One of the layers that I have highlighted
is internal plane number two Gerber data.

So Altium automatically
creates those extensions
and assigns a description to them
right here inside the file.

Even if your fabrication house
doesn't have Altium installed
on their CAM department's computers,

you can still create this
fabrication drawing in draftsman
and include this layer stack legend.
And it's going to include

all of those file
extensions automatically,

and that's going to help
eliminate any ambiguity
in which layers belong in which locations
in the PCB stackup.

Thank you very much, Alexander,
for the great question.

I'm always happy to
answer these questions.
And if you ask a great question,

it just might end up
in one of these videos.

Make sure to hit the like
button, hit the subscribe button,

leave your comments and
questions in the comment section,
or of course find me on LinkedIn
and send me a question there.
And last, but not least,

don't forget to call
your fabricator, folks.
We'll see you next time.
(dramatic music)

title: Creating Stacking Stripes for PCB Fabrication: Altium Tutorial
